title: Compassion can grow
hook: short compassion trainings changed responses to others' pain in lab studies (Klimecki et al., 2013)

segments.voice: Yesterday: wu wei, acting without forcing. Your line: start with small things.

Your aunt who remembers every birthday was born that way. Your coworker who never notices anyone was born that way too. That's how people talk about it: some people are just kind, a trait like height or eye color, and you got whatever you got. It's a comfortable idea, because it lets everyone off the hook. But a group of researchers in Germany wondered whether it was true. Could a short training change how a person responds when they see someone else in pain? They taught people a very old practice, then put them in a brain scanner and showed them videos of people suffering.
screen: `SOME PEOPLE ARE JUST KIND.` → `A TRAIT, LIKE EYE COLOR?` → `THE RESEARCHERS WONDERED.`

segments.voice: First, two things that sound alike. Empathy is feeling with someone: their pain lands in you. Compassion is feeling for someone: warmth toward their pain, and a wish for it to ease. The researchers found the difference matters. In studies by Olga Klimecki, Tania Singer and colleagues, people first trained in empathy alone, resonating with others' distress. After watching the videos, they reported feeling worse, and brain areas linked to pain became more active. Then they trained in compassion, the warm wish. Their brain responses shifted toward areas linked to care, reward and connection, and they reported more positive feeling, even while watching the same suffering. Short trainings made a measurable difference, in the lab. Second, what they practiced: loving-kindness, the Buddhist practice called metta, from this path's visit to Buddhism. You bring someone to mind and silently wish them well, first someone easy, then a stranger, then someone difficult. Buddhists call compassion karuna, the wish that others be free from suffering. Third, the caution. These are lab studies with small groups, measuring feelings and brain signals. Another study found training helped people give a little more in a sharing game, but nobody has shown that a weekend turns anyone into a saint. The honest claim is modest: it's trainable. And that matters. If compassion is a trait, burnout means you've run out. If it's a skill, feeling flooded by other people's pain may mean you're practicing empathy without the warmth. You can add the wish. Compassion can grow, the way a muscle does, slowly, with use.
screen: `EMPATHY FEELS WITH. COMPASSION FEELS FOR.` · `EMPATHY HURT. COMPASSION WARMED.` · `METTA: WISHING SOMEONE WELL.` · `MODEST, BUT TRAINABLE.` · then, large: `COMPASSION CAN GROW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a stranger, maybe someone you saw today, at the checkout, behind the wheel, on the train, whose name and day you don't know. Silently wish them well in the plainest words you have: may your day get easier, may you be well. If you like, add one more stranger; notice any warmth, and don't worry if there isn't much.
Karuna, the Buddhist wish that others be free from suffering, not a fixed trait but a skill that can be trained.
Your line: silently wish them well. One stranger in passing is one rep. That's day three hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: In loving-kindness practice, drawn from Buddhism, people bring someone to mind and silently wish them well, moving from a loved one to a stranger to someone difficult; researchers have used short versions in lab studies of compassion.
